meta.title: Your first month at Larchfield
meta.description: A handbook for new engineers: what to do in week one, how a change reaches production and how on-call works.
meta.author: Larchfield Software, Engineering enablement

summary: Week one is for getting set up and shipping one small change, not for learning the whole system. Every change reaches production the same way: a reviewed pull request, a green pipeline, a canary and an automatic rollout. You join the on-call rota in week six, after two shadow shifts, and the first rule of a page is to acknowledge it and ask for help early.

meta.question: What should I do in my first week?
meta.title: Week one

answer.headline: Get your accounts and laptop working, meet your buddy and team, and ship one small change to production by Friday. Nobody expects you to understand the whole system yet.
answer.text: Your manager has picked a starter ticket that touches the real deploy pipeline but cannot hurt customers. Shipping it teaches you more about how we work than a week of reading.
points: Your buddy is your first stop for any question, however small
Setup should take one day; if it takes longer, the guide is wrong, so tell us
Reading the code is fine, but pairing on a real ticket is faster

items.title: Laptop, accounts and welcome
items.text: Collect your laptop at 09:30, run the setup script and join the 11:00 welcome session with People team.

items.title: Meet your team
items.text: Sit in on stand-up and planning. Your buddy walks you through the services your team owns.

items.title: Local environment running
items.text: Run the app and its tests locally. Pick up your starter ticket and pair on it with your buddy.

items.title: First pull request
items.text: Open your pull request, respond to review and watch the pipeline run.

items.title: First change in production
items.text: Merge, watch the canary and tell the team channel it is live. Lunch with the team is on us.

items.v: An engineer on your team, for your first 6 weeks

blocks.title: Ask early
blocks.label: Tip
blocks.body: If you have been stuck for 30 minutes, ask. A question in #eng-help usually gets an answer within the hour, and it often shows us a gap in the docs.

items.q: When do I get production access?
items.a: Read-only access to logs and dashboards in week one. Write access to production systems comes with on-call, after your shadow shifts.

items.q: What if my starter ticket is not done by Friday?
items.a: That is fine. The aim is to go through the whole process once; a ticket that turns out bigger than expected is useful too.

items.q: Do I need to read all the architecture docs?
items.a: No. Read the overview for your team's services. The rest makes more sense once you have shipped something.

meta.question: How does a change get from my laptop to production?
meta.title: How we ship

answer.headline: Every change goes through a reviewed pull request, a green pipeline and a 5% canary for 15 minutes before it rolls out to everyone. Rollback is automatic if error rate or latency rises.
answer.text: We deploy small changes many times a day. The pipeline is the only way into production: nobody copies files to a server or edits a live database by hand.
points: One approval from a code owner is needed to merge
Main is always deployable; unfinished work hides behind a feature flag
A typical change is live 35 minutes after merge

blocks.title: The path to production
blocks.caption: Every merge to main takes this path. A failed check at any stage stops the change.

meta.title: Deploy pipeline
meta.description: A pull request is reviewed and tested, merged to main, built once, deployed to staging, then to a canary and finally to all servers.

steps.title: Overview
steps.description: The stages every change passes through.

steps.title: Review and merge
steps.description: A code owner approves and the change merges to main.

steps.title: Canary
steps.description: 5% of traffic sees the new version for 15 minutes while error rate and latency are compared.

steps.title: Rollout
steps.description: A healthy canary rolls out to every region.

items.note: of deploys; each one is a bug caught early

items.note: above this, the owning team fixes it first

items.title: Keep it small
items.text: Under 400 changed lines. Split refactors from behaviour changes.

items.title: Say why
items.text: The description explains the problem, not just the change, and links the ticket.

items.title: Test it
items.text: New behaviour has a test. Say how you checked it by hand, if you did.

items.title: Flag what is unfinished
items.text: Anything users should not see yet goes behind a feature flag, off by default.

blocks.title: Do not deploy on Friday afternoon
blocks.label: House rule
blocks.body: The pipeline stays open, but changes merged after 15:00 on a Friday wait for Monday unless they fix an incident. Fewer people are around to notice a slow-burning problem over the weekend.

blocks.title: What blocks a merge
rows: Fix the test or the code; never skip it
Upgrade the package, or ask #security for an exception
Ask in your team channel for a reviewer

meta.question: How does on-call work, and what do I do when I am paged?
meta.title: On-call basics

answer.headline: You join your team's on-call rota in week six, after two shadow shifts. When paged, acknowledge within 5 minutes, open an incident channel and ask for help early: nobody handles a serious incident alone.
answer.text: Each team runs its own rota of one week at a time, Monday 10:00 to Monday 10:00. A secondary engineer backs up the primary, and an incident commander from the wider rota joins anything SEV-1 or SEV-2.
points: On-call pays a flat weekly allowance plus time off in lieu for night pages
Your job is to restore service first; finding the root cause comes later
Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 gets a blameless review within 5 working days

items.title: Acknowledge within 5 minutes
items.text: If you do not, the page goes to the secondary, then to your manager.

items.title: Judge the severity
items.text: Use the severity table. If unsure, pick the higher level; you can lower it later.

items.title: Open an incident channel
items.text: Type `/incident new` in Slack. It creates the channel, a timeline and a status page draft.

items.title: Stabilise
items.text: Roll back the last deploy, switch off the feature flag or fail over. Restore service before you debug.

items.title: Hand over or close
items.text: Write what you did in the channel, so the next person or the review can follow it.

blocks.title: Severity levels
rows: Most customers cannot use a core feature, or data is at risk
A core feature is broken for some customers
Degraded but usable, or an internal tool is down

blocks.title: Escalating is not failing
blocks.label: Remember
blocks.body: Paging the secondary or an incident commander at 03:00 is exactly what they are there for. The reviews we learn most from are the ones where someone asked for help in the first ten minutes.

items.text: Two shadow shifts with an experienced engineer
Install the paging app and test a page to your phone
Read the runbooks for your team's top five alerts
Confirm you can reach production consoles from home
Swap shifts in the rota tool, not in chat, so the pager follows

answer.headline: Severity is about customer impact now, not how hard the fix looks. Pick the higher level when in doubt; lowering it later costs nothing.
points: Data loss or a security exposure is always SEV-1
A problem that will become customer-facing within an hour is treated as if it already is
Severity sets who is paged and how often we update the status page
